title: Tower Builder
context: Grade 4. An adult sees towers of sums and products. What is actually being settled is what makes a tower correct. The page shows one tower that adds all the way up and one that multiplies all the way up, and then asks which of six towers are correct without ever saying that a tower keeps to one operation. Mixed box by box, every one of the six printed towers works. The tool states the rule the page's own two towers follow, one operation for every box, and makes checking every box against it the job.

writeup.why: Build a number tower up from the bottom by adding or by multiplying, and check every box to decide whether a tower is correct.
writeup.look: A tower of boxes, each resting on two below, with an operation switch at its foot and a check walk that climbs it box by box.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Tower Builder' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the boxes filled or checked against the boxes the tower holds, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each box is filled or passed by a walk, and the second is fixed at the size of the tower. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tower stands in the left of the working area, three to five boxes wide at the bottom and one box narrower in each row above. A box is 130 by 72 with 28 between neighbours. Each row sits 14 above the one below, shifted along by half a box and half a gap. A bottom row of five spans 762 at 100,566, and a tower of five rows reaches up to 222. Every box rests visibly on exactly two boxes, with a short near-black strut from each of them up to it. The sign rail draws the chosen sign in every gap between neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up. The operation switch stands at the foot, 262 by 60 at 350,656, and must be set before any box takes a number. Other operation stands beside it, 200 by 60 at 632,656. Tapping an empty box lights the two boxes it rests on, and the box slot takes the number for it. The box keeps a number only if the chosen operation makes it from those two, and hands it back otherwise with both still lit. The ledger stands down the right of the working area, 270 by 416 at 876,222, one line to a box, and writes the working in words as each box is reached. The check walk climbs a filled tower box by box from the bottom row up. At each box it lights the two boxes underneath, then the box above, and writes the working in the ledger. A box that does not follow keeps its reddish purple light after the walk has moved past, and the walk carries on to the top rather than stopping. Missing box leaves any one box blank at any level, as an empty outlined box, to be found from the boxes around it. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across, with an add key and a times key above them that set the switch as well as the sign. On the third and fourth phases two verdict keys stand under them, every box follows and a box breaks it, so a verdict can be given by press. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A box is never drawn resting on one box or on three, and never off centre over its pair. A box that does not sit squarely on its two is a box whose pair can be misread, and the whole of this tool is which two boxes make which box.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last tower the child built, its sign drawn between every pair of neighbours, and the tower they checked with the box that broke the rule still lit.

phases.win: each row fills in turn and the top box lands last
phases.does: taps an empty box, adds the two boxes it rests on, and works up one row at a time
phases.goal: each box is made from the two boxes side by side beneath it
phases.says: Which two boxes hold this one up? Add them together.
phases.check: Away from the screen: build a tower of your own on three, five and two. What is at the top?
phases.feels: every box stands on its own two, and the tower is built one row at a time from the bottom
phases.hands: Stand four paper cups in a row with a sticky note on each, carrying a number. Build the next row of cups on top, each resting on two, and have the class say which two cups hold each new cup up. Write each new cup's number as the sum of those two. Then ask what the top cup would hold if every bottom number were simply added together, and compare that with the top the tower actually makes.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which two boxes hold this one up? Second rung, the phase's: what do those two make when they are added? Third rung: the tower is cut to a bottom row of two and one box on top, and the child fills that one box. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the top box looks like the total of the tower, and adding every number in sight is what a total has always meant.
wrong.move: adds the whole bottom row and writes that total in the top box, thirty for six, nine, four and eleven.
wrong.screen: the top box is tapped and lights the two boxes it rests on, not the bottom row. The child's thirty stays written beside the tower. The rows are then built up one at a time with the working written in the ledger, and the top lands on fifty-six.

wrong.why: the rows are staggered, and the eye slides back to the pair it has just used.
wrong.move: fills a box from the wrong pair, sliding one box along, so the box over nine and four gets six add nine again.
wrong.screen: tapping the box lights the two it rests on, nine and four, and the child's fifteen is handed back with those two still lit. The struts from nine and four up to the box light as well, and the ledger writes nine add four.

phases.screen: an adding tower with its bottom row filled and every box above it empty
phases.soWhat: Each box in an adding tower is the sum of the two boxes side by side beneath it.
phases.concept: Two neighbours make the box above

phases.win: the times sign shows between every pair and the top box fills
phases.does: multiplies each pair of neighbours and fills the tower up to the top
phases.goal: a multiplying tower has the same shape and multiplies in every box
phases.says: This tower multiplies. Which two boxes hold this one up?
phases.check: A multiplying tower has two, three and two along the bottom. What goes in the two boxes above, and at the top?
phases.feels: the same tower and the same pairs, and only the sign in the gaps has changed
phases.hands: Build a second cup tower beside the first, and turn a card at its foot that says times. Have the class multiply each pair of neighbours and write the product on the cup above. Put a one in the bottom row on purpose, and ask what a number times one makes before anyone writes it. Then set the two towers side by side and ask what is the same and what has changed.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which sign does this tower use? Second rung, the phase's: what do the two boxes below make when they are multiplied? Third rung: the tower is cut to two bottom boxes and one box above, and the child multiplies once. The number keys and the sign keys stay open.

wrong.why: the first tower of the lesson added, and the first row is where the old habit is still in the hand.
wrong.move: adds the bottom pair out of habit, writing four above three and one, and multiplies only higher up.
wrong.screen: the box slot hands the four back with the times sign drawn between three and one, and the sign rail draws the times sign again in every gap of every row. The ledger writes three times one. The child's four stays beside the box.

wrong.why: one is the smallest number in the row, and multiplying by it seems as though it should make things small.
wrong.move: writes one above three and one, taking times one to leave only the one.
wrong.screen: the ledger lays out three groups of one counter each, and they are counted aloud. The child's one stays beside the box, and the count stands next to it.

phases.screen: the same tower with the switch turned to multiplying and a new bottom row filled
phases.soWhat: A multiplying tower has the same shape as an adding one, and each box is the product of the two below it.

phases.win: the walk lights each box in turn and one box keeps its light, its working written beside it
phases.does: runs the check walk box by box and stops on the box that breaks the rule
phases.goal: a tower is tested by checking each box against the two below it, one at a time
phases.says: Check each box against the two below it. Does every box follow?
phases.check: A tower has two, six and three at the bottom, then eight and nine, then seventeen. Check each box aloud.
phases.feels: one box at a time, the two below it named every time, and the top box last of all
phases.hands: Swap cup towers between groups, planting one cup whose number breaks the rule before the swap. Each group checks every cup from the bottom row up, saying aloud the two cups below it and what they make. Ask how many cups they had to check before they could say the tower did not follow its rule. Then ask why checking only the top cup would not have been enough.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which two boxes hold up the box you are checking? Second rung, the phase's: does that box follow the same sign as the rest? Third rung: the tower is cut to its bottom row and one box, and the child checks that single box. The number keys and the verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: the top box is the answer the tower was built to reach, so if it adds up the tower seems to be finished.
wrong.move: checks only the top box, finds that eight add ten is eighteen, and calls the whole tower correct without testing each box.
wrong.screen: the check walk climbs from the bottom row and tests each box in turn, writing its working in the ledger. The box holding ten keeps its reddish purple light, because two add five is seven. The top box's working is written too, and it adds, so both stand together.

wrong.why: the first tower met in class added, and adding is the operation a stack of boxes suggests.
wrong.move: tests every tower by adding, so a tower that multiplies all the way up is called broken at its first box.
wrong.screen: the walk with adding lights the first box, because two add three is five, not six. Other operation then runs the same walk with the times sign, and every box follows. Both walks stay written side by side in the ledger.

phases.screen: a tower that arrives already filled, with one box that does not follow
phases.soWhat: A tower is tested by checking each box against the two below it, and one box that breaks the rule is enough.
phases.concept: Checking a tower box by box

phases.win: each walk runs the whole tower, and the boxes its sign cannot make stay lit
phases.does: walks the tower with adding, then with multiplying, and decides whether either works all the way up
phases.goal: a tower is correct only when one operation works for every box, from the bottom row to the top
phases.says: Try one sign for every box. Does it work all the way up?
phases.check: A tower has two, five and one at the bottom, seven and five above, and twelve at the top. Does one sign work for every box?
phases.feels: one sign, set once at the foot, and every box in the tower answering to it
phases.hands: Show the tower page's two towers side by side, one that only adds and one that only multiplies. Then build a cup tower that multiplies to make its middle row and adds to make its top, and ask whether it is one of those two kinds. Say the rule aloud and say where it comes from. The page's own towers keep one operation all the way up, and a tower is correct when one operation works for every box.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which sign makes the first box? Second rung, the phase's: does that same sign make every other box? Third rung: the tower is cut to two rows, and the child runs one walk with each sign. The verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: every box can be made from its two by one sign or the other, and the page never says a tower keeps to one.
wrong.move: accepts a tower whose middle row multiplies and whose top adds, because each box works with some operation.
wrong.screen: both walks run the whole tower. With adding, five add one is six, not five, and that box stays lit. With multiplying, five times three is fifteen, not eight, and the top stays lit. Neither walk runs clean, and both stay in the ledger.

wrong.why: a box that works with both signs looks as though it belongs to both kinds at once.
wrong.move: calls the tower page's multiplying tower mixed, because two and two make four by adding and by multiplying.
wrong.screen: both walks run on that tower, and the box holding four stays unlit in both, because it follows either sign. The adding walk lights box after box, starting beside it, where two add one is three, not two. The multiplying walk runs clean all the way to sixty-four at the top.

phases.screen: a tower that multiplies in one row and adds in the next, with both walks waiting
phases.soWhat: A tower is correct only when one operation works for every box, from the bottom row to the top.
phases.concept: One operation all the way up

writeup.delight: The first phase, once the top box has landed. Any number in the bottom row can then be tapped and changed, and the tower rebuilds itself upward from it. Only the boxes resting on that number, directly or through the rows between, make themselves again, one row at a time; every box it cannot reach stays still. The top box lands last with its new number. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase an adding tower stands with its bottom row filled, every box above it empty and the switch already set to adding. On the second the same frame stands with the switch turned to times and a new bottom row filled. On the third a tower arrives already filled, with the check walk waiting at its foot and the ledger empty. On the fourth a filled tower stands with both walks waiting side by side at its foot. The running count at the top left holds the boxes filled or checked against the boxes the tower holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the lowest empty box, or the switch, or the second row's first box, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which two boxes hold it up. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any bottom row of up to five numbers, either operation, with the check walk and the other operation control open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding towers, multiplying towers, checking a tower box by box, and whether one operation works for every box from the bottom row to the top.
voiceLines: A tower of empty boxes, and a switch at its foot. Choose the sign first.
Which two boxes hold this one up? Add them together.
This tower multiplies. Which two boxes hold this one up?
Check each box against the two below it. Does every box follow?
Try one sign for every box. Does it work all the way up?
Another tower. One sign, and every box made the same way.
Free play. Any bottom row, either sign, with both walks open.
Tap the box again, and look at the two boxes holding it up.
Every tower built from the bottom, and every box checked against one sign.

observations.why: A box is made from the two it rests on, and the rows are staggered so each box sits on its own pair.
observations.soWhat: A tower is built up one row at a time, each box from its own two.
observations.observe: Each box lit exactly two boxes when it was tapped, and never the box beside it.

observations.why: Which two boxes make a box does not depend on the operation.
observations.soWhat: Adding towers and multiplying towers are built the same way, and only the operation changes.
observations.observe: The multiplying tower had the same shape and the same struts, and only the sign in every gap changed.

observations.why: Every other box followed the rule, so the top could come out right with one box wrong beneath it.
observations.soWhat: A tower is checked box by box, because the top box alone cannot show a broken box below it.
observations.observe: The walk left one box lit after passing it, while the top box above it still added up.

observations.why: One row followed adding and another followed multiplying, so no single sign made every box.
observations.soWhat: A tower is correct only when one operation works for every box, from the bottom row to the top.
observations.observe: On the tower that switched signs, each walk left a different box lit, and neither walk ran clean.

source_tool.name: Tower Builder
source_tool.blurb: Build a number tower up from its bottom row by adding or by multiplying, then check every box against one operation.

serves.exercise: identifying which of the six number towers are correct

source_tool.description: A tower of boxes stands in the middle of the stage, widest at the bottom and one box narrower in each row above, with every box resting on the two boxes side by side beneath it. An operation switch at the foot of the tower is set to adding or to multiplying before any box can be filled, and the sign it shows is drawn between every pair of neighbours in every row, so the whole tower visibly keeps to the one operation chosen. The child fills a box by tapping it, which lights the two boxes it rests on, and then writing the number; the box keeps the number only if it is what the chosen operation makes of those two. A check walk tests a tower that arrives already filled, box by box from the bottom row up, lighting the two boxes underneath and the box above in turn and writing the working beside it, and any box that does not follow keeps its light on after the walk has moved past. An other operation control runs the same walk with the other sign, so a box that works only by the other operation is seen for what it is, and a tower that changes operation between rows fails both walks. A box can be left blank at any level and found from the boxes around it, and the bottom row takes numbers of the child's own.
source_tool.art_direction: A tower of boxes on a switch / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Tap the box again, and look at the two boxes holding it up.
voice.onNext: Another tower. One sign, and every box made the same way.
voice.opening: A tower of empty boxes, and a switch at its foot. Choose the sign first.
voice.onFinish: Every tower built from the bottom, and every box checked against one sign.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any bottom row, either sign, with both walks open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Two neighbours make the box above
Checking a tower box by box
One operation all the way up

placement.where: After a tower of paper cups has been built with sticky notes, one group adding and one multiplying, and before the printed towers are judged. The tool is what holds a whole tower to the one operation set at its foot and walks it box by box, which a tower drawn on paper leaves to the reader.

answer_key.rule: Each box in a number tower rests on two boxes side by side, and it is made from those two. In an adding tower it is their sum; in a multiplying tower it is their product. The page's two towers each keep to one operation all the way up, so a tower is correct when one operation works for every box, from the bottom row to the top. To check a tower, test each box against the two below it, one at a time, with the same operation throughout. One box that does not follow makes the tower not correct, even when every other box does, and a tower that adds in one row and multiplies in the next fits neither kind. A missing box is found from the boxes it rests on or from the box it helps to make.
answer_key.wrong: The check walks the tower again from the bottom row, one box at a time, lighting the two boxes underneath and writing the working beside each box, and stops with its light on the first box that does not follow. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Each box is the sum of the two boxes side by side beneath it: 6 + 9 = 15, 9 + 4 = 13 and 4 + 11 = 15.
The next row adds those: 15 + 13 = 28 and 13 + 15 = 28.
The top box adds the last two: 28 + 28 = 56.
items.answer: 15, 13 and 15, then 28 and 28, then 56 at the top
items.question: An adding tower has 6, 9, 4 and 11 along its bottom row. Fill the boxes above, one row at a time, up to the top.
items.checkpoint: Each box is made from the two boxes it rests on, one row at a time.
items.misconception: Adding a box to the box beside it in the same row, instead of using the two it rests on.

steps: Each box is the product of the two beneath it: 3 x 1 = 3, 1 x 2 = 2 and 2 x 2 = 4.
The next row multiplies those: 3 x 2 = 6 and 2 x 4 = 8.
items.answer: 3, 2 and 4, then 6 and 8, then 48 at the top
items.question: A multiplying tower has 3, 1, 2 and 2 along its bottom row. Fill it up to the top.
items.checkpoint: A multiplying tower has the same shape as an adding one; only the operation changes.
items.misconception: Adding in the first row out of habit and then multiplying higher up.

steps: Test the first middle box: 6 + 2 = 8, so it adds. Multiplying would give 6 x 2 = 12, so it does not multiply.
Test the second middle box by adding: 2 + 5 = 7, not 10. Ten is 2 x 5, so this box multiplies.
The top adds, 8 + 10 = 18. One box breaks the adding rule, so no one operation works for every box.
items.answer: No. 8 is 6 + 2 and 18 is 8 + 10, but 10 is 2 x 5 and not 2 + 5, so the box holding 10 breaks the adding rule
items.question: A tower has 6, 2 and 5 at the bottom, 8 and 10 in the middle, and 18 at the top. Check each box. Does every box follow one operation?
items.checkpoint: Check every box, not only the top, because one box can break the rule while the rest keep it.
items.misconception: Checking only the top box, which adds up, and calling the whole tower right.

steps: Try adding on every box: 5 + 1 = 6, not 5, so adding fails in the middle row.
Try multiplying on every box: 5 x 1 = 5 and 1 x 3 = 3 work, but 5 x 3 = 15, not 8, so multiplying fails at the top.
Neither operation works for every box. The tower changes operation on the way up, so it is not correct.
items.answer: No. The middle boxes multiply, 5 x 1 = 5 and 1 x 3 = 3, but the top adds, 5 + 3 = 8. A correct tower uses one operation for every box
items.question: A tower has 5, 1 and 3 at the bottom, 5 and 3 in the middle, and 8 at the top. Every box works with some operation. Is it a correct tower?
items.checkpoint: A tower is correct only when one operation works for every box, from the bottom row to the top.
items.misconception: Accepting the tower because each box works with some operation, when it switches from multiplying to adding.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: An adding tower has 8, 5 and 7 along the bottom. What goes in the two boxes above them, and at the top?
An adding tower has 14, 16, 20 and 5 along the bottom. What number is at the top?
items.final_answer: 127: the rows above the bottom are 30, 36 and 25, then 66 and 61, then 127

items.question: A multiplying tower has 2, 5 and 1 along the bottom. What goes in the two boxes above them, and at the top?
A multiplying tower has 3, a missing box and 2 along the bottom, and 12 and 8 above them. What is the missing box, and what is at the top?
items.final_answer: 4, because 3 x 4 = 12 and 4 x 2 = 8, and the top is 12 x 8 = 96

items.question: A tower has 3, 4 and 6 at the bottom, 7 and 10 in the middle, and 17 at the top. Check each box. Does it add all the way up?
items.final_answer: Yes. 3 + 4 = 7, 4 + 6 = 10 and 7 + 10 = 17, so every box adds

items.question: A tower has 2, 3 and 4 at the bottom, 6 and 12 in the middle, and 72 at the top. Check each box. Which operation does every box use?
A tower has 2, 4 and 3 at the bottom, 6 and 7 in the middle, and 42 at the top. Is the tower correct, if one operation must work for every box?
items.final_answer: No. The middle row adds, 2 + 4 = 6 and 4 + 3 = 7, but the top multiplies, 6 x 7 = 42, so no one operation works for every box

items.question: Build a tower of your own on 2, 3 and 5, multiplying in every box. What goes in each box above the bottom row?
items.final_answer: 6 and 15, then 90 at the top, because 2 x 3 = 6, 3 x 5 = 15 and 6 x 15 = 90

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets the tower to adding or to multiplying before any box is filled
draws the chosen sign between every pair of neighbours in every row
lights the two boxes a box rests on when it is tapped
takes the number for the lit box and keeps it only if the operation makes it
tests a filled tower box by box from the bottom row up
runs the same walk with the other sign
leaves a box blank at any level to be found from the boxes around it
takes the child's own numbers for the bottom row

teaching_notes: Build one adding tower and one multiplying tower out of paper cups and sticky notes before the tool is opened, and make the class say, for each box, the two boxes it rests on. Then say the rule out loud, and say where it comes from. The page's own two towers each keep to one operation all the way up, and a tower is correct when one operation works for every box. The page never states it. It shows its two towers and then says towers can be made with as many numbers as we like, which a careful child can read as allowing both signs in one tower. Mixed box by box, every one of the six printed towers in Exercise 10.1 works, and two of them even keep to one operation within each row, one multiplying below and adding on top and the other the other way round. So without the rule the question has no answer, and with it the answer is the three towers that keep one sign all the way up. Check box by box from the bottom, and name the two boxes being tested each time. A child who checks only the top box will pass a tower whose top happens to add up.
generation_prompt: Build a number tower tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tower of rounded boxes stands centred in the working area, three to five boxes wide at the bottom and one box narrower in each row above, every box drawn resting visibly on exactly two boxes beneath it. An operation switch at the foot of the tower must be set to adding or to multiplying before any box accepts a number, and the chosen sign is drawn between every pair of neighbouring boxes in every row. Tapping an empty box lights the two boxes it rests on; the number pad down the right takes the child's number, and the box keeps it only if the chosen operation makes it from those two, handing it back otherwise with the two lit boxes still lit. A check walk tests a tower that arrives already filled, box by box from the bottom row up, lighting the two boxes underneath and the box above in turn and writing the working beside it; any box that does not follow keeps its light on after the walk has moved past. An other operation control runs the same walk with the other sign. A missing box control leaves any one box blank to be found from the boxes around it, and an own bottom row control takes the child's own numbers. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Choose adding or multiplying first. Tap an empty box. Use the two boxes under it. Write what they make. Check every box, from the bottom row up. Keep one sign for every box.
